Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A crew member on a U.S.-flagged cargo ship captured by pirates off the coast of Somalia is suing his employers, claiming they sent him into pirate-infested waters without adequate protection, his attorney said Monday. Abduwali Abdukhadir Muse has been charged with piracy in federal court in New York. Richard Hicks of Royal Palm Beach, Florida, a crew member on the Maersk Alabama, filed suit Monday against Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited, according to the attorney, Terry Bryant. A spokeswoman for Mobile, Alabama-based Waterman Steamship Corp. said she did not know about the suit and did not immediately comment. A spokeswoman for Maersk Line Limited did not immediately return a call from CNN seeking comment. The Maersk Alabama was hijacked by pirates April 8. Hicks, working as chief steward and preparing food for other crew members, heard over the loudspeaker that pirates were on board, and he and other crew members gathered in the ship's engine room for nearly 12 hours, according to a news release from Bryant. "The engine room was dark and hot, maybe 130 degrees," Hicks said in the news release. "We were all cramping up with heat stroke symptoms when we were able to take a pirate hostage and tried to negotiate the return of our captain." The pirates promised to exchange Capt. Richard Phillips for the pirate hostage, but reneged on that agreement, the news release. Phillips offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew. He was held on a lifeboat until U.S. Navy snipers on a nearby ship fatally shot three pirates, rescued Phillips and arrested a fourth pirate. The ship's owners -- the two companies -- knowingly exposed their employees to danger and took no steps to provide appropriate security and safety for the crew, Bryant alleges. "Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited chose to rely on the United States military and taxpayers to provide after-the-fact rescue operations," Bryant said in the news release. "This choice caused substantially more cost and risk to human life than what would have been incurred by defendants had they provided appropriate levels of security in the first place." Hicks is seeking at least $75,000, and "reserves the right to amend this pleading for a certain amount in the future, as it is too early to determine the maximum amount of plaintiff's damages," according to the suit. Hicks is still suffering from injuries as a result of the incident and is afraid to return to work, the news release said.

**Mobile, Alabama (CNN) —** A crew member aboard the *Maersk Alabama* has filed a lawsuit against Waterman Steamship Corp. and Maersk Line Limited, alleging the companies failed to protect sailors from the threat of Somali piracy before the cargo ship was hijacked.

Richard Hicks claims the companies knowingly sent the vessel through dangerous waters off the coast of Somalia despite repeated warnings about pirate activity, according to the complaint. The lawsuit alleges the ship’s route and security precautions exposed its crew to an unreasonable risk.

Somali pirates boarded the U.S.-flagged *Maersk Alabama* in April 2009 as it carried humanitarian cargo toward Kenya. Crew members eventually regained control of the vessel, but the pirates escaped in a lifeboat with Capt. Richard Phillips as a hostage.

The standoff ended several days later when U.S. Navy snipers killed three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was taken into custody.

Hicks alleges he suffered physical and psychological injuries because of the attack and is seeking damages for negligence, lost income, medical expenses and emotional distress. The complaint’s allegations have not been proven in court.

Waterman Steamship employed members of the vessel’s crew, while Maersk Line Limited operated the ship. The lawsuit contends both companies had a duty to provide a reasonably safe workplace and take appropriate anti-piracy measures.

Representatives for Waterman and Maersk did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

# Maersk Alabama Crewman Files $75,000 Claim Over Pirate Hijacking

**HOUSTON —** Richard Hicks, a crew member aboard the *Maersk Alabama* when Somali pirates seized the U.S.-flagged cargo ship, has filed a claim seeking at least $75,000 from the vessel’s owners and operators, alleging they knowingly sent the ship into pirate-infested waters without adequate protection.

The complaint names Maersk Line Ltd. and Waterman Steamship Corp. as defendants. Hicks alleges the companies failed to provide a safe workplace, ignored repeated warnings about piracy off the Horn of Africa and did not take sufficient steps to protect the crew.

The allegations have not been proven in court. The companies have maintained that the safety of their crews is a priority.

## Ship seized off Somalia

The case stems from the April 8, 2009, hijacking of the *Maersk Alabama* while it was carrying humanitarian food aid toward Mombasa, Kenya. Four Somali pirates boarded the ship roughly 300 miles off the Somali coast in the first successful seizure of an American-flagged commercial vessel by pirates in about two centuries.

The attackers briefly took control of the bridge and captured Capt. Richard Phillips and several other sailors. Most of the 20-member American crew, however, escaped into the ship’s lower compartments.

Crew members shut down the engines and electrical systems, leaving the pirates unable to operate the vessel effectively. Barricaded in the engine-room area in stifling heat and darkness, they communicated with one another, monitored the pirates’ movements and worked to regain control of the ship.

Members of the crew eventually overpowered and restrained one of the hijackers, Abduwali Muse. They attempted to exchange him for Phillips, but the deal broke down.

## Phillips taken hostage

As the standoff deteriorated, Phillips was forced into one of the ship’s enclosed lifeboats with the remaining three pirates. The hijackers fled the *Maersk Alabama* with Phillips as their hostage, beginning a four-day confrontation with U.S. naval forces.

The destroyer USS *Bainbridge* reached the scene and began negotiations. Other U.S. vessels and specialized military personnel subsequently joined the operation.

On April 12, Navy SEAL snipers aboard the *Bainbridge* shot and killed the three pirates after commanders concluded that Phillips faced an imminent threat. Phillips was rescued unharmed apart from the effects of his captivity. Muse, who was aboard the American destroyer receiving medical treatment and participating in negotiations, was taken into U.S. custody and later prosecuted in federal court.

## Lawsuit focuses on advance warnings

Hicks’s claim centers not only on the pirates’ actions but also on decisions made before the *Maersk Alabama* entered the region. The suit alleges the defendants knew that piracy posed a serious and well-documented danger near Somalia but failed to alter the ship’s route, provide armed security or put adequate protective measures in place.

His lawyers contend those alleged failures exposed Hicks and the rest of the crew to an avoidable risk of injury, captivity and death. The filing seeks compensation for physical and psychological harm, medical expenses and other damages connected to the ordeal.

A request for at least $75,000 can also serve as a jurisdictional threshold in federal civil litigation; the final amount, if any, would depend on evidence, negotiations or a court judgment.

The case could test how far shipping companies’ duties extend when merchant vessels operate in waters known for piracy. It also underscores the divide between the crew’s widely praised resistance aboard the *Maersk Alabama* and questions over whether corporate and operational decisions left them unnecessarily exposed in the first place.

**Maersk Alabama crewman sues employers over Somali pirate attack**

HOUSTON (AP) — A crew member of the Maersk Alabama has sued the ship’s operator and the company that supplied its crew, alleging they failed to adequately protect seamen from Somali pirates despite warnings about the danger, his attorney said.

Houston lawyer Terry Bryant said the lawsuit was filed on behalf of crewman Richard E. Hicks against Maersk Line Ltd. and Waterman Steamship Corp. The complaint accuses the companies of negligence for sending the U.S.-flagged cargo ship through pirate-infested waters without sufficient security or protection.

The allegations have not been tested in court.

Somali pirates boarded the Maersk Alabama on April 8 off the Horn of Africa. The crew retook control of the vessel, but the pirates escaped in a lifeboat with Capt. Richard Phillips as a hostage. U.S. Navy snipers killed three pirates and rescued Phillips four days later.

Bryant said Hicks suffered physical and emotional injuries during the attack. The lawsuit alleges the companies knew or should have known of the piracy threat and should have provided armed security, an escort or other safeguards.

Maersk Line said it had not reviewed the lawsuit and therefore could not comment on its allegations. Waterman Steamship did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The suit seeks damages for medical expenses, lost income, pain and suffering and emotional distress.
